problem_markdown: For a real initial value $x_1$, define $x_{n+1}=x_n(x_n+1/n)$. Prove that exactly one initial value produces $0<x_n<x_{n+1}<1$ for every $n\ge1$.
solutions_markdown:
Let $F_n(t)$ be the $n$th term starting at $t$. Each $F_n$ is a strictly increasing polynomial on $[0,\infty)$ with nonnegative coefficients and $F_n(0)=0$. Define $a_n,b_n$ by $F_n(a_n)=1-1/n$ and $F_n(b_n)=1$; thus $a_1=0,b_1=1$.

The recurrence gives $F_{n+1}(a_n)=1-1/n<1-1/(n+1)$ and $F_{n+1}(b_n)=1+1/n>1$. Hence $a_n<a_{n+1}<b_{n+1}<b_n$. The nested closed intervals have a common point $t$, which lies strictly between every pair of endpoints. Therefore $1-1/n<F_n(t)<1$, giving positivity and $F_{n+1}(t)>F_n(t)$.

For uniqueness, convexity and $F_n(0)=0$ imply
$$1-1/n=F_n(a_n)\le\frac{a_n}{b_n}F_n(b_n)=\frac{a_n}{b_n}.$$
Thus $b_n-a_n\le b_n/n\le1/n$, so their common intersection is a single point. Conversely any initial value satisfying the requested inequalities must have $x_n>1-1/n$, hence belong to every interval. This proves exactly one exists.
